reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Describes an amnestic dementia of the very old driven by limbic-predominant TDP-43 proteinopathy
Clinically mimics amnestic Alzheimer's disease, with insidious, progressive episodic memory impairment
Increasingly recognised in individuals in their eighth decade and beyond
Progression tends to be more gradual than in typical Alzheimer's disease
Frequently coexists with Alzheimer pathology and hippocampal sclerosis, contributing to mixed dementia
Amyloid biomarkers are typically negative when it occurs in isolation, which helps distinguish it from Alzheimer's disease
A neuropathological staging scheme tracks TDP-43 spread from the amygdala to the hippocampus and then the middle frontal gyrus
reference.pathophysiology: Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy is characterised by accumulation of abnormally phosphorylated TDP-43 protein within limbic structures, beginning in the amygdala and spreading to the hippocampus and neocortex, often accompanied by hippocampal sclerosis. This proteinopathy disproportionately affects the oldest old and produces a predominantly amnestic syndrome. It is a distinct entity from Alzheimer's disease but frequently coexists with it, and the combination of pathologies tends to accelerate cognitive decline.
additionalDifferentials: Mild cognitive impairment of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Neuropsychological testing documenting an amnestic profile
MRI brain assessing hippocampal and medial temporal atrophy
Amyloid PET or CSF amyloid and tau biomarkers to gauge the contribution of Alzheimer pathology
Investigations to exclude autoimmune or limbic encephalitis where onset is atypical
Vascular risk assessment and structural imaging for coexisting cerebrovascular disease
redFlags: Subacute or rapidly progressive amnesia suggesting autoimmune limbic encephalitis
Focal neurological signs indicating an alternative structural cause
Onset in a much younger patient than expected for this age-related entity
reference.prognosis: This is a slowly progressive dementia; when it occurs in isolation the course tends to be more indolent than Alzheimer's disease, but coexisting Alzheimer or vascular pathology worsens the outlook. It is a neuropathologically defined entity, so definitive confirmation remains post-mortem, and management is supportive with attention to safety, function and carer support.
pitfalls: Assuming all late-life amnestic dementia is Alzheimer's disease and not considering this entity, especially in amyloid-negative patients
Interpreting negative amyloid biomarkers as excluding a neurodegenerative cause of memory loss
Overlooking mixed pathology in the very old
Expecting a definitive antemortem diagnosis, which is not yet possible
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Nelson et al., consensus report defining limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (Brain)
